body: A bass player came back for his amplifier and has not picked it up. The hall has been empty for twenty minutes, a quarter past nine on a Thursday; the chairs are stacked against the wall and the urn has been switched off. He is standing in the half-dark playing a figure of four notes, over and over, slightly differently each time. The woman who was locking up has sat down at the piano and put something underneath it. Neither of them has said what the tune is. There is nobody left in the building to hear it, and it goes on for another seven minutes.

What those two were doing had no audience, no running order and no finish time, and it was the most attentive either of them had been all evening. Nobody was delivering anything. They were listening to each other, and the music was what the listening sounded like.

Jazz is an odd fit for a worship band on paper. It has no obvious congregational function, most of it has no words at all, and its reputation is for cleverness — which is not a virtue anybody is looking for in this context.

It is worth being precise about the word performing, because the objection to it here is not a complaint about excellence. To perform is to carry a thing through to completion — to furnish forth something that was settled beforehand. A performance is decided in advance and then executed in front of people, and the better it is, the less the room in front of it can change it. That is not a criticism — most of the music on this dial works exactly that way. But it does mean that a performance can be, in the strict sense, finished before anybody arrives. The people in the room are the occasion for it. They are not inside it.

The band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 frequencies, of which 46 are on air today. Nearly every one of them plays music that was written down, arranged, argued over and finished long before it was recorded. HM 372.10 is assigned to Inspire Jazz and is not yet on air — the number is held for it, which is the only honest thing to say about a station that is still being built.

Improvised music is expensive in a way that is easy to miss. A take cannot be tidied afterwards, because the second player was answering the first, and correcting the first line leaves the second replying to something that is no longer there. There is no version to tighten and no arrangement to sell on. What you keep is one particular evening, mistakes included, because the mistakes are load-bearing. It is kept anyway, and the reason is not musical taste. The whole form is people listening to each other closely enough to respond in real time. There are worse descriptions of a church.

That kind of attention has become rare, and not because people got worse at it. Almost everything now arrives finished. The sermon is clipped to its strongest ninety seconds, the song is front-loaded so that it survives a scroll, and the conversation is a series of statements posted at each other with no obligation to answer the one before. It is what happens when everything is prepared in advance for an audience that might leave, and the effect is that fewer and fewer things are now made in the presence of the people they are made for.

The shape itself teaches something. A tune states its head, and then the players take it in turn, and the ones who are not soloing have the harder job — holding the form, marking where the chorus turns, leaving space that somebody else is about to use. Then all of them come back to the head together, which only works if every one of them kept counting through the parts where nothing was asked of them. That is a skill, and it is not a musical one. It is the skill of holding a shape while giving way.
You are not listening to a finished thing. You are listening to people deciding, in front of you, and then having to live with what they decided.

The rehearsed and arranged version has real virtues and they should be stated properly. A congregation can join in, because the song is the same as it was last week. Nothing collapses in the second verse. The words were weighed by somebody who was not tired, which is more than can be said for most of us at half past ten on a Sunday morning. A form built to be repeated is how anything at all gets carried across a generation. But the one thing it cannot do is be altered by the room it is standing in. It arrives having already happened.
A performance is finished before you get there. A conversation is not.

A woman who runs the sound desk at a church in a converted showroom has a son of seventeen who plays the drums badly and improving. On a Sunday in February the guitarist misses an entry — he has turned two pages at once — and there is a bar and a half where the song is simply not there. Her son does not fill it. He drops to the rim, quietly, and waits, and holds the tempo until the guitarist finds his place again, and the congregation notices nothing whatever. Afterwards nobody mentions it, including her. She thinks about it for most of the week. He has never once given way to her in a kitchen.
Nothing in that required him to be good. It required him to be listening to somebody else at the exact moment when the obvious thing to do was to keep playing his own part.

This form has a real fault and it should be said plainly. Improvised music can disappear up its own cleverness. There are solos played for the other musicians and for nobody else, choruses that go round twice more than they should, and long stretches where a person listening in an ordinary kitchen has no idea what is being attempted or when it is going to stop. You cannot sing along with it. A good deal of it is, frankly, wallpaper.

The wandering is not a failure of the format, though. It is the format, visible. A thing that can surprise you can also bore you, and both possibilities come out of the same property — that nobody knew what the next minute contained. Music that is incapable of boring you is incapable of startling you as well. Every form that has ever caught somebody sideways has had a wide margin of ordinary minutes round it, and the margin is not waste. It is the price of the moment when the second player answers.

So the case for it is not that jazz is sophisticated worship. It is that almost everything else arrives at a room having already been decided, and this is the one common form that does not. It is made in the presence of the people it is made for, by players who keep counting through the parts where nothing is asked of them and leave space for somebody else on purpose. That is a description of a form. It is also, uncomfortably closely, a description of a congregation.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

46 of the 121 frequencies are carrying programming now, and they are not all doing the same job. There is music, which is most of the band — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns, rap, ambient and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer. There are the children’s stations. And there are 40 international frequencies hosted in 29 languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. What there is least of, so far, is music made up on the spot, because that end of any band is the smallest and the most expensive to keep.

So start at HM 311.50 — Riddim and Rhyme. It is Zariah Inspire’s Afro-Caribbean catalogue, reggae and dancehall and soca and Afrobeats married to teaching hymnody and gospel-soul, and the programme at eight in the evening is called the Yard Session. That is the reason it is named here. A yard session is not a concert. It is what happens when the people who can play are in the same place and somebody starts, and the music itself has always been a conversation held between a bass and a drum with everybody else answering. It is not the wordless music this article opened with; there is a great deal being said on that frequency. But it is where you can hear players listening to each other, which is the only quality being argued for.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have, and you can add the page to a home screen if you want it closer to hand. Do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

Then do what the bass player did with his amplifier still sitting by the door: stay a little longer than the reason you came for. Put HM 311.50 on this evening while you are washing up, and do not sit down in front of it. Let it go on underneath the room. Somewhere in the second week a phrase will arrive that nobody arranged for you, at an hour when you were not paying attention, and you will notice that you have stopped what you were doing in order to listen. That is the whole of it.
